## Mr. Chatterbox

The Victorian Gentleman chatbot

If I could pick out any science-fictional device to have in my garage, I would choose a time machine. The dangers of temporal paradox notwithstanding, I have always wanted to travel into the past. Modernity is cognitively saturating. The assumptions and expectations that we live by are difficult to shake. But by encountering the past we can glimpse different ways of living, and thereby reconsider how we navigate our own lives. To quote C.S. Lewis, “we need intimate knowledge of the past… because we cannot study the future, and yet need something to set against the present.”

The threads linking the past and the present have been on my mind a lot lately. In the last few months my life has undergone changes both profound and quotidian. In June, my wife and I welcomed our son into the world. In July, we moved our family from Urbana to Chicago, Illinois (if you have ever considered moving houses with a 6-week-old infant, here is my advice for you: don’t). Suddenly, I have found myself in a new role, navigating a new set of priorities, setting my own past against my radically altered present. There’s nothing like becoming a parent to make you reconsider your priors.

While all this was going on, I was also experiencing a flurry of interest and activity connected to the Mr. Chatterbox project. The beta iteration of Mr. Chatterbox was enthusiastically received on social media, written up by Simon Willison , and even became the basis for a class at Emory University. Several other “vintage” models were released around the same time as Mr. Chatterbox, including talkie and TypewriterLM . AICHR (Artificial Intelligence for Cultural and Historical Research) released the “ Chronologic ” benchmark for vintage language models in September. It turns out that people aren’t just interested in LLMs as a means to more efficiently write emails or manage a schedule, but as a way to encounter the past and explore humanistic questions—to use them, one might say, as a time machine.

I realized I needed to bring the project to its completion, not only because of the interest in it, but because I have a baby who is every day becoming more social and more aware, and so will need more and more of my time. I needed to finish my metaphorical time machine, before the only way I could finish this project was with a literal time machine. With help from the community, the engineering prowess of Claude Code, some paternity leave, and a grant from The Cosmos Institute , I spent months turning that vision into reality.

Today, I am incredibly proud to introduce the Mr. Chatterbox model family, a set of language models trained entirely on 19th century British text. The family consists of four fully-trained base models: Mr.Chatterbox-345M , Mr.Chatterbox-500M , Mr.Chatterbox-1.2B , and Mr.Chatterbox-2.7B . All of the base models are trained to Chinchilla-optimality for their size using the Llama framework. Furthermore, I have trained Mr.Chatterbox-2.7B-Chat , a chat-tuned version of 2.7B trained on fine-tuning data drawn from the corpus. I am releasing my training code on Github. Finally, I am releasing my fine-tuning dataset, Mr.Chatterbox-SFT , for anyone who may be interested in using it. Unlike the previous iteration of Mr. Chatterbox, there is very, very little “synthetic” data in the training mix: 97.2% of the model’s learned SFT material is directly sourced from period text, with the remaining portion either period text with a small edit (e.g. "Hello Mr. Micawber" replaced with "Hello Mr. Chatterbox") or generated by the Mr. Chatterbox model itself (rejection sampling).

First, Some Numbers

Before I begin with my qualitative description of how I built the model, I do want to acknowledge some quantitative metrics: when I ran it against AICHR's Chronologic-EN 1.0 benchmark, Mr.Chatterbox-2.7B-Base would be the second-best model on the leaderboard, just under the larger Talkie-13B in the overall score, and matching or topping larger models on constrained generation and knowledge and inference accuracy. Instruction tuning cost the model a lot at knowledge & inference, but boosted close accuracy and constrained generation. Interestingly, the Chronologic benchmark draws from texts between 1831 and 1930, and Chatterbox has a knowledge cutoff of 1899, but overall accuracy barely moved across the 20th-century dateline (35.2% before 1900, 34.3% after), because relatively few of the questions measured post-1900 period knowledge.

These numbers being what they are, I would consider the Mr. Chatterbox project a success, but training these models was by no means easy. As I have said before, I don’t work for a big lab or university. There were many pitfalls, failures, and frustrations along the way. But maybe you, oh reader, can learn from my efforts (or laugh at my foibles) as I built a better Mr. Chatterbox.

Designing a Victorian Gentleman

The initial Mr. Chatterbox checkpoint was both small (at 345 million parameters) and undertrained (on just 2.93 billion tokens). The model was also fine-tuned on synthetic material—that is, material written by a modern LLM in a Victorian style. While I had done the best I could to scrape away the most egregious LLM-isms in my synthetic data, it still spoke like a contemporary stereotype of a Victorian gentleman.

At first, I thought I would have to train my new checkpoint on synthetic material as well. I considered student-teacher architecture , or the History-SelfInstruct method employed by the team behind TypewriterLM. But eventually, I decided on something more radical: building a model where every word emitted was learned from period text. I wanted every assistant-side turn in the model’s supervised fine-tuning data to consist of text extracted from my corpus, and not authored by a modern LLM. Ultimately, I was able to assemble a dataset where 97.2% of the assistant-side turns were sourced from period text, with the remainder either lightly-edited or generated by Mr. Chatterbox itself (more on that later).

I also knew that I would need a lot more pretraining data. I had some choices to make about how I would assemble it. This was maybe the most important decision in the entire project. The pretraining corpus determines how a language model understands the world. I could have built a pretraining corpus that contained every document ever published in the 19th century that I could get my hands on. Or, I could have built a corpus that included including contemporary literature about the Victorian era (like Hobsbawm) to give the model a more comprehensive viewpoint. Both choices would have allowed me to build a larger model, and language model performance gets better as models get bigger .

But I was not interested in optimizing my model to beat general benchmarks. I wanted to re-embody the lost Victorian mindscape. I wanted the model to have a unique perspective, and having a point of view implies that there are things that you cannot see. Including a bunch of contemporary histories of the 19th century or documents published in 1800’s America would dilute the unique “Victorian gentleman” viewpoint that I wanted to embody.

Furthermore, I knew—from analyzing over 40,000 real user turns from my beta model’s usage logs—that most users were not using Mr. Chatterbox as a “helpful digital assistant,” which is the persona of most LLMs. Instead, users were employing Mr. Chatterbox as, well, a time machine—a way to interact with the past. Factual queries and opinion solicitations made up over 51% of user sessions, with greetings another 15%. 12% of turns consisted of task requests (such as “write me a letter” or “suggest a birthday present to my wife”), with intents like multi-turn follow up questions and abuse rounding out the rest.

In other words, people were interested in interacting with an erudite and clever Victorian conversationalist, as opposed to a diligent clerk. As I began to assemble my training corpus, my rough heuristic became: would an educated gentleman living in London in the Victorian era be able to access this document? That would include straightforwardly Victorian material like Dickens’ novels and Parliamentary records, as well as Victorian-era editions of Shakespeare’s plays and the letters of Cicero, both of which were written by non-Victorian figures but would have been widely available at the time.

I ended up restricting my dataset to public-domain volumes of 19th century works published in the British Isles (Britain as well as Ireland, Scotland, and Wales). In addition to my original dataset from the British Library, I also pulled material from the Internet Archives, Project Gutenberg, Institutional Books, the Wellcome Collection/UK Medical Heritage Library, Nineteenth-Century Serials Edition, Old Bailey Proceedings, Hansard, and House of Commons Parliamentary papers. But my largest dataset came from the HathiTrust Digital Library (thank you to Dr. Ted Underwood at UIUC for HathiTrust help!).

The majority of my data came from the late-Victorian era (post-1870’s), with a small portion being published pre-Victorian (pre-1837). Nearly 20% of the data is classified as “Language & Literature” (i.e. fiction), with other big portions including history, philosophy, and medicine. As we’ll see later, training on billions and billions of tokens of late-Victorian fiction and philosophy gave the model a strong prior to continue any input text, rather than engage in dialogue.

Because much of my text had been digitized, I had to go through a few rounds of data cleaning to remove digitization notices and metadata. I generally trusted the metadata for the sources I drew from to ensure no period leakage, though in a few instances I had to scan documents with a local language model to ensure a valid publication date. My final dataset consisted of a little over 55 billion tokens after tokenization with my custom tokenizer. That gave me sufficient data for a 2.7-billion parameter model, which is about the size of Microsoft’s Phi-2 , a “small-but-mighty” model notable for outperforming larger models when it was released a few years ago.

Pretraining

My previous experience of pretraining was easy, but this round proved to be much more challenging. While training the 345M and 500M parameter models took only a few hours on an 8-GPU cluster, 1.2B needed 20 hours, and 2.7B needed three days. I began to hit uptime reliability problems on Vast.AI. The training process crashed several times on these larger models, often in the middle of the night.

Fortunately for me, I have an infant, meaning that I am frequently awake between the hours of 1 and 6 AM. It was nonetheless frustrating to stand in my office at 3 AM and re-start a training process that had been stalled for four hours while juggling a bottle and a baby. Even as a new dad, I managed to pretrain all four models in about 4 days. I felt heroic. It would be smooth sailing from here… or so I thought.

While assessing the pretrained checkpoints, I discovered that the crashes had engendered a much larger problem: every time the script crashed, training restarted from the beginning of the corpus. So, even though the output log indicated that training was progressing successfully, the model was in fact beginning from the top of the corpus with each restart. With each model having had several stops and restarts because of uptime problems, the model had trained on a small portion of data over and over again, and not on the diverse corpus I had assembled. This meant the models were no good: I had to retrain them.

I eventually managed to rent a sufficiently-reliable cluster to complete pretraining for all four model sizes, while also having Claude Code rewrite the script so that, in the event of a crash, the training process would start from where it stopped, and not from the top.
